articleTitle: Application of IEEE 1584 to IEC Equipment
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: IEEE 1584 provides models and an analytical process to enable the calculation of the predicted incident thermal energy and the arc-flash boundary. The Guide provides typical dimensions and working distances for different types of electrical distribution equipment where arc-flash hazards exist. However, this typical data is generally focused on equipment manufactured to ANSI/NEMA standards. This paper will highlight the differences when applying the IEEE 1584 models and analytical processes to equipment manufactured to IEC standards.

articleTitle: Petrochemical Plant Turnaround Study Case: Planning, Executing, Findings and Lessons Learned
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: This document provides a case study of a Petrochemical Plant Turnaround. The power distribution aspects in planning a preventive maintenance outage includes the definition of critical loads, generator usage plan, communication with parts involved, switching plan, training of crew, affected personnel and third parties. In addition, it shows how the execution stage occurred: work permits, area isolation, switching, protecting energized panels against mistakes, the findings that need to be fixed before re-energization, and notes for future turnarounds. It also shows lessons learned from the whole process.

articleTitle: Analysis of Power Quality Monitoring Methods in Industrial Distribution Systems
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: Measurement and monitoring power quality is becoming increasingly important across industrial plants. There are various parameters that are used to quantify power quality and different methods for monitoring these parameters to ensure efficient and proper operation of equipment connected to the industrial distribution system. As industrial distribution networks are becoming increasingly complex, with loads from variable speed drives fed by pulse width modulation (PWM) inverters along with local generation from inverter based distributed energy resources (DERs), the need for power quality monitoring is essential to maintaining operational resilience. This paper analyzes some types of power quality disturbances, such as harmonics, flicker, etc. and how they affect industrial distribution systems. This paper also analyzes different techniques and methods used to measure power quality, such as CBEMA curves, EN 50160 reporting, waveform capture, and other web-based methods, and explains how each method focuses on specific areas of power quality. Power quality monitoring can be taken a step further with analytics and identification of specific circuits or devices which are the source of these disturbances to the distribution system. This allows for corrective actions to be taken effectively without hampering overall efficiency and functionality of the system. It is important to understand how the different monitoring methods provide varying levels of visibility into the system’s operation and efficiency, which will then allow preemptive action to be taken.

articleTitle: Why are Class I/Division 1 and Zone 1 Induction Machines Employed less and less in Industries Today?
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: For installation of induction machines (motors) in Class I/Division 1 or Zone 1 hazardous locations, it is important to realize that, due to higher risk of release, Division 1 (Zone 1) requirements are much more stringent than Division 2 (Zone 2). Therefore, the equipment needs corresponding explosion protection methods. There are two types of protection widely used in these locations; they are explosionproof and pressurized enclosure.This paper summarizes those requirements and the applicable standards for the US and Canada For Class I/Division 1, explosionproof is often the most cost-effective technique as the only other alternative, pressurization, requires a significant additional ancillary equipment to support pressurization. However, the explosionproof technique is limited in size due to the physical strength limitations of a large "explosion pressure withstanding enclosure." As the testing often involves multiple samples, it is impractical for a one-off design to employ the explosionproof design.For Zone 1, a flameproof "d" motor is similar construction to an explosionproof motor, but increased safety "e" becomes a practical solution for midsize motors, with only the exceptionally large motors employing pressurization "p".In some cases, changes to the implementation of the process can result in a change to the area classification resulting in a Class I/Division 2 or Zone 2 area classification, allowing, in many cases, ordinary location machines specially in North America, with a far simpler assessment and testing regimen, and less costly installation.

articleTitle: The Impact of Changing Medium Voltage Switchgear Standards on The Application of Dedicated Motor Buses
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: A large oil and gas company decided to adopt IEC standards for Medium-Voltage Switchgears. During the front-end engineering design (FEED) stage of various projects, while conducting short-circuit analysis and device-duty evaluation using power-system simulation commercially available software (henceforth will be referred to as software), challenges related to the application of large, direct-on line, motors on dedicated motor buses were faced. The capability of the motor’s circuit breaker to handle the interruption of through-fault currents with high dc offset became an area of concern with the IEC-rated breakers. This put a limitation on how large of a motor can be started across the line in terms of horsepower. This limitation was never faced with the same application when ANSI rated circuit breakers were utilized. A market research and analysis were conducted by reaching out to different manufactures to assure that this limitation will not create obstacles during the detailed-design phase of the project. Results analysis will be presented along with recommendations on how to tackle the technical issues associated with the application of IEC standards on dedicated motor medium-voltage buses.

articleTitle: Performance and Drive Characteristics of Slotless Axial Flux Motors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: Axial Flux Motors (AFM) can be more suitable for some applications than radial flux motors due to volume density characteristic. Slotless motors can facilitate the manufacturing process that requires core lamination in the same direction as the motor rotation. Removing the slots from the motor and placing the windings in the air gap (air gap winding) have an important impact on motor performance and drive characteristics, mainly due to the low winding inductances values. The behavior of a motor with a low inductance value driven by a frequency inverter was evaluated. The motor was tested with and without an output filter for comparative purposes. The behavior of the motor in the laboratory test was also observed by finite elements analysis.As a solution for the design, a switching frequency of 15 kHz was proposed instead of the standard 4 kHz, reducing the current harmonic by 51,2%. Also, an external inductor can reduce the current harmonic by 43,7%. In both alternatives, the temperature and motor losses were significantly reduced.For an application study, a coreless motor was dimensioned for a ventilation application. To fulfill the specification. With the proposed motor, it was possible to reduce 51% of the motor axial length.

articleTitle: Electrical Obsolescence Management: Proactive & Data Driven Mitigation Strategies
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: A company engineering team addressed the challenge of managing obsolete and/or aged electrical equipment assets in over 1000 substations. Given that some of the electrical equipment has been in service for 40+ years and the company estimated to spend nearly $1B over the last 10 years to replace obsolete equipment, it was critical that the engineering team manage the risk posed by aging and obsolete equipment to prevent unscheduled or prolonged outages. Previous work (i.e., IEEE PCIC papers in 2010 and 2014) outlined the company’s Obsolescence Management Program (OMP) methodology and execution strategies, equipment condition assessment program, OMP program challenges, and obsolescence mitigation strategies for low voltage (600 V class) and medium voltage (5 kV and 15 kV class) equipment. The paper presents advanced mitigation strategies devised by the engineering team for high voltage equipment (34.5 kV to 230 kV). In addition, the paper will present the OMP’s progress and the risk-based evaluation developed to prioritize replacement projects.

articleTitle: Understanding the Relationship Between Total Harmonic Distortion and Total Demand Distortion in IEEE STD 519-2022: A Practical Discussion for Compliance Evaluations
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: When trying to apply the harmonic limits of IEEE Std 519-2022, there can often be confusion on the difference between Total Harmonic Distortion (THD) and Total Demand Distortion (TDD), and when each value is used. The intent of this paper is to provide clarity and direction on how to apply the Standard’s Current Distortion Limits as they were intended in a way that is practical for real world projects. This paper will outline how to apply the limits at an existing site and during the design stage of a new installation/project. This paper describes how to determine the maximum demand load current without the need to wait until after the system has been installed and operated for many months. Using this value, one can then calculate the appropriate demand distortion to compare against the IEEE Std 519 demand distortion requirements.

Author Keywords: ITDD or TDD (Current Total Demand Distortion)

articleTitle: Electrical Distribution System Optimization Using Reliability Analysis
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: This paper details a methodology to optimize electrical distribution systems using a production-based approach to electrical reliability in the Oil and Gas industry. The objectives of the optimization are to reduce downtime caused by electrical distribution outages, improve distribution system selectivity based on production impact maps, and reduce system power losses. This approach utilizes probabilistic electrical reliability analysis combined with Oil & Gas production data to optimize the distribution system topology by prioritizing production as opposed to electrical loads. A cost-effective solution for downtime reduction can be achieved by simulating different distribution system topology improvements. This can be done after adding field collected historical distribution equipment failure data, and wells and facility production data to existing electrical models. Additionally, a production impact map is created to optimize the location of protection devices (reclosers, fuses) prioritizing the protection of high producing sites.

articleTitle: Review of Energizing High Power Medium Voltage AC Drives
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: This paper first introduces the well known high power medium voltage AC drive topologies. Starting with types using a capacitive DC link voltage source inverter fed from a drive isolation transformer and multi-pulse rectifier the many approaches of initial energization techniques are summarized. Therewith, a common knowledge basis is established and the adverse reactions of direct on line energizing at full-voltage are exemplified in regards to the magnetic and DC link capacitive inrush. Based on that, the energizing of a three-level neutral point clamped topology using a soft-magnetization technique that mitigates the aforementioned stresses on the equipment is presented.

articleTitle: Replacing Lead-Acid and Nickel-Cadmium Stationary Batteries with Lithium-Ion – It’s Not a Simple Swap
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: The rapid advancement and adoption of lithium-ion batteries in battery electric vehicles and battery energy storage systems has people considering replacing their existing lead-acid and nickel-cadmium stationary batteries with lithium-ion. The potential space and weight savings can be substantial however safety, reliability, and cost are major considerations. Lithium-ion batteries pose fire risks and increased building fire loads that lead-acid and nickel-cadmium batteries do not present. Additionally, lithium-ion batteries have reliability issues, not present in lead-acid and nickel-cadmium batteries, which must be addressed. Inserting lithium-ion batteries into traditional lead-acid and nickel-cadmium roles is not a simple battery swap. The additional costs and risks must be carefully evaluated when considering a swap from traditional technologies to lithium-ion batteries.

articleTitle: A Review Of Metering Safety Concerns
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: This paper discusses the arc hazard safety issues surrounding industrial and utility revenue meters. The requirements and exceptions are discussed surrounding the use of NFPA 70E – Standard for Electrical Safety in the Workplace, ANSI/IEEE C2 – The National Electrical Safety Code (NESC), and OSHA – The Occupational Safety and Health Administration. Concerns are presented regarding the use and applications of electrical codes and regulations for both industrial/commercial use in comparison with that of the electric generation, transmission, and distribution utilities. The author presents a safety concern with regard to the safe installation and maintenance of electric revenue meters. This paper is directed to all electric utilities including investor owned, municipal and Rural Electric Utilities.

articleTitle: Four Quadrant Medium Voltage Drives
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: Medium voltage drives require regenerative capability for applications like lifts, conveyors with overhauling loads and other applications that require torque control or fast deceleration. One method to provide regeneration at low cost and low complexity in medium voltage drives is with the use of six-step control method. While the control of front-end semiconductor devices is simple, the resulting input currents have much higher distortion during regeneration as compared with the currents during motoring. During the last decade, the cascaded H-bridge (CHB) inverter has become the topology of choice for medium voltage (MV) motor drive applications. In this paper a CHB topology with low inverter count of nine is considered with six-step control. A new method to control the front-end devices of the individual inverters is proposed. Implementation of the method with a multi-pulse transformer is described. This method is shown, through simulations and circuit measurements, to improve the input current distortion of the input currents during regeneration while meeting the limits recommended in the IEEE-519 Standard.

articleTitle: SYNC or ASYNC – How to Start a Synchronous Motor Driving a Reciprocating Compressor
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: Slow speed reciprocating compressors are typically rigidly coupled to single bearing synchronous motors. The compressor load during starting is seldom above 30% of the motor rated torque. In addition, synchronous motors have a relatively low starting current and a relatively high torque-peramp ratio. Consequently, most applications allow for an across-the-line start. There are however occasions where an adjustable speed drive is used for starting. In these instances, the user has two options to consider, start as an induction motor (asynchronously) or start as a synchronous motor with the main rotor field energized from zero speed. This paper will discuss the merits of each of these options for both new installations as well as retrofits. It will consider the views of the motor designer, ASD designer, and end user as well as provide guidance on how to evaluate each option.

articleTitle: Do ARC Mitigating Systems Really Work?
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: Electrical equipment, fitted with arc quenching technologies, have been employed and have been providing personnel and equipment protection in many global installations for over two decades. This technology continues to evolve, advance, and provides significant reduction of arc incident energy. However, a limiting factor has become the actual standards which define some of the fundamental aspects of its design and applications. This work outlines how the present generation of arc quenching technologies continue to reduce arc incident energy and improve the safety within switchgear, motor control centers or control panels. Very detailed testing results will provide conclusive evidence of a superior level of protection to not only the protected equipment and process, but also to personnel as well. The factory and site acceptance testing criteria for arc mitigation systems, to guarantee the correct operation of the system, will be discussed as well. Common myths and misconceptions surrounding arc quenching technologies, such as the system current impact expectations when using arc quenching technologies, are also covered.

articleTitle: Lessons Learned From A 35KV Submarine Power Cable Replacement
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: With today’s increased focus on reducing emissions, a significant amount of new and existing oil and gas companies around the world are working towards installing and/or replacing segregated generation centers by a centralized approach [12] [13] [14] and feeding the required facilities using a submarine power cable (SPC).Considering the current cost and lead time for these SPCs, it is important to have a good set of multidiscipline specifications, and standards to rule the technical design and testing of the SPCs, as well as having procedures in place to guide the selection, transportation, installation, and commissioning for these SPCs. Even though the industry comes with a significant set of standards to guide the SPC design, not all of them cover the full spectrum of requirements needed for this specialized design and installation. Therefore, complementing specifications with multiple standards is necessary. As the study case shows, over-specifying the technical aspect can confuse manufacturers and add unnecessary complexity to the SPC design. Additional consideration of the issues involved in transportation, testing and installation are required to avoid jeopardizing the final solution.This paper presents the lesson learns from one study case which covers an SPC replacement project from initial technical design through manufacturing, transportation, and installation.

articleTitle: Complying with NFPA 70B and Minimizing the Total Cost of Ownership of Medium Voltage Switchgear using Condition Monitoring Technologies and Data Analytics
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: The NFPA 70B Standard for Electrical Equipment Maintenance specifies that electrical equipment shall be maintained in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions and applicable codes and standards, and that the equipment owner shall implement an overall electrical maintenance plan (EMP). Medium voltage (MV) distribution equipment can operate safely for many years and remain in good condition if installed in appropriate environments and properly maintained. Most organizations, even today, resort to the maintenance strategies of fix upon failure or a time- or usage-based maintenance program, and this is reflected in their EMP. However, advances in sensor technologies coupled with the dramatic growth in the information infrastructure of Internet of Things (IoT) and data analytics capabilities has opened new possibilities to rethink equipment maintenance based upon continuous monitoring of the equipment health. Such monitoring brings benefits of reduced operational costs through predictive maintenance and reduced downtime. An additional important benefit is an increase in personnel safety and reliability due to reduced onsite service and human interaction. In this paper we show how condition monitoring and data analytics technologies can reduce the total cost of ownership while complying with NFPA 70B.

articleTitle: The Drive to Electrify: Benefits of Electrification of Fossil Fuel-Fired Process Heating Equipment
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: The electrification of fossil fuel-fired process heating equipment represents a paradigm shift in the industrial landscape, driven by the imperative to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, enhance energy efficiency, and ensure compliance with environmental regulations. A key aspect of this transition is the electrification of traditional fossil fuel-fired process heating equipment. By replacing fossil fuels with electricity, industries stand to achieve substantial reductions in carbon emissions, contributing to global efforts to combat climate change. Electrifying fossil fuel equipment reduces air pollutants and minimizes the carbon footprint of industrial operations, making it an integral part of the green energy transition. This paper explores the advantages and benefits of electrification as it pertains to industrial electric heating as an effective solution to improve energy efficiency and meet environmental mitigation targets.

articleTitle: Lessons Learned Commissioning a Relay-Based Synchronous Motor Excitation Control System
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: Synchronous motors are a vital asset in many industrial processes. Although typically requiring more complex controls and maintenance than standard induction motors, synchronous motors provide operational benefits that often render them the preferred driver for numerous specialized manufacturing and processing applications. This paper presents a practical example of a control solution that enables automatic excitation regulation of a synchronous motor field winding – a microprocessor-based motor protection relay that provides a closed-loop feedback control signal to the silicon-controlled rectifier (SCR) exciter to automatically regulate the excitation supply current, which in-turn enables automatic regulation of the motor power factor (PF) and efficiency. In addition, this paper will discuss the various lessons learned during the update and associated startup commissioning of an aged excitation control system to the above solution for two synchronous motors driving ball mills in a large cement plant.

articleTitle: Advantages of Paralleling Transformers at Industrial Sites with a Communication-based Paralleling Method
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: To address the increase in load at industrial facilities, an additional transformer can be added and paralleled with the existing transformer. When the transformers are equipped with On-load Tap Changers (OLTC), the loads should be balanced between the paralleled transformers to avoid circulating current and resulting heating due to overloading of one of the transformers. Classic circulating current and circulating reactive current paralleling methods have been used successfully for many years at industrial sites and electric power utilities. The circulating current and circulating reactive current methods of paralleling use paralleling balancing current transformers and their associated current loops with complex wiring from many breaker status contacts between the paralleled transformers. This additional paralleling equipment and most of the wiring between the transformers and breakers required by the circulating current and delta VAr methods can be eliminated with a communication-based Peer-to-Peer paralleling method. This paper describes the basic concepts of paralleling transformers and provides a detailed description of the communication-based paralleling scheme. This method consists of using a high-speed Peer-to-Peer communication link to implement a paralleling scheme for two or more transformers. The information passed between the transformer controls is communicated via Ethernet-based IEC 61850 Generic Object Oriented Substation Event (GOOSE) messaging protocol. This paper will discuss the advantages of using the communication-based paralleling scheme.

articleTitle: State of the Art Technologies for Liquid Immersed Power Transformer Online Monitoring
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: Liquid Immersed Power transformers are critical components of electrical power distribution systems, and their reliable operation is essential to maintaining system stability and reliability. Continuous Online monitoring of power transformers can identify incipient problems before they lead to outages, production losses, or other safety and environmental impacts. Switching from a time-based maintenance to a condition-based maintenance approach can reduce downtime and costs of transformer maintenance. This paper reviews the technologies available for power transformer online monitoring, as included in the latest IEEE and CIGRE documents [1],[2],[3],[5],[6],[7],[8]. The paper will discuss the key monitoring parameters for online transformer monitoring. The paper also discusses the challenges of online monitoring of power transformers, such as the need for reliable sensors, the need to interpret data correctly, and the need to integrate monitoring data with other information to identify potential transformer failures.

articleTitle: Storage of Electricity in the Form of Energy Using Hydrogen
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: There are many sources of energy used today to generate power in the form of electricity. The ideal vision for the future is to find a way to store energy in its purest form for extended periods of time. Today, industry has chemical and electrolytic means to store electricity, but only for a short duration, and its transportation is mostly grid-based. Hydrogen (H<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>), in the stable form of water (H<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O), is present in large quantities and is well-suited for the energy supply chain as an energy storage mechanism and secondary energy source. 1 kg of H<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> contains as much energy as 2.1 kg of natural gas or 2.8 kg of gasoline [1]. H<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> is produced by electrolysis, which can be modeled by: Electricity + Water = Hydrogen + O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>. The challenge is to make this process more efficient by using less expensive renewable electrical energy.

articleTitle: Turbine Replacement With Electrical Drivers – Evaluating Options
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: The transition of steam and gas turbines to electric motor drivers provides viable options to address existing and future regulations on CO2 emission savings and lower operating expenses. The replacement of the turbines can take place in existing (so-called "brownfield" replacements) inland as well as offshore based facilities. With the existing plant layout of a brownfield installation, all possible electrical driver configurations may not be feasible, such as geared solutions.This paper will give an overview of the existing technical solutions for electrical drivers and especially focusing on the challenging topics to be considered with a turbine replacement. Since application requirements are different from case to case, the optimum solutions will vary based on technical and economic criteria, including the specific location details of the application. The paper will provide help to plan the scope of work on the compressor or pump train, the selection of the best solution based on technological criteria plus the impact of each train solution option on different areas such as Capital Expense, Operating Expense, Environment / Health & Safety, Reliability and Serviceability. Furthermore, interface-handling is described, like rotor-dynamic topics and foundation interaction.Finally, an important consideration is the required planning/preparation time for a brownfield turbine replacement. The time slot for the regular plant shut down is typically fixed based on five to eight year schedules. It is therefore important to start the preparation in time to be able to meet the envisaged turnaround schedule with the best solution.

articleTitle: Relay-Based Electrical Signature Analysis for Incipient Motor Failure Detection - Field Successes
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: Unexpected motor failures often cause a significant impact to facility operations. To improve personnel safety, minimize unplanned shutdowns, reduce maintenance expenses, and maximize operational revenue, industry worldwide has largely shifted to an enhanced approach to motor maintenance - one that focuses on proactive, preventative maintenance rather than reactionary repair. One prevalent motor failure detection technique used is Electrical Signature Analysis (ESA). While historically cost-prohibitive to apply to smaller machines or less crucial processes, technological advancements have given rise to various much more economical and accessible options to implement ESA technology. This paper will discuss one option - the application of ESA as part of an existing motor protection & control relay. The general concept of ESA will be outlined as well as the benefits ESA incorporated into a protection relay offers and the types of mechanical faults it can effectively detect. Several case studies will be presented, including successful incipient failure detections examined at a petroleum refinery, a pulp and paper facility, and a petrochemical plant.

articleTitle: Implementing Cybersecurity for Industrial-Connected Products
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: This paper provides an overview of current cybersecurity standards. It presents a case study on applying cybersecurity standards, practices, and certifications to a cybersecurity program covering a range of industrial-connected products. It reflects on where the industry is regarding cybersecurity risk — highlighting current standards and certification programs and looking at upcoming standards and the regulations related to them.As part of the overview of cybersecurity standards, this paper examines current and upcoming region-specific requirements, the complexities this cause, efforts to harmonize relevant standards, and how to best focus on meeting those requirements as a global manufacturer. Particular attention is paid to the requirements of the International Society of Automation (ISA) / International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) 62443 (within the framework of National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) SP 800-53) and the specific obligations that need to be met by component and equipment manufacturers.The case study examines how manufacturers can use certifications to minimize risk by demonstrating alignment with security best practices and standards. It also reflects on how to use a certification program to help manufacturers streamline compliance burdens while meeting customers’ needs, concentrating on the significant challenges, strategies for implementation and how the certification bodies involved in these regulations can assist in overcoming those challenges through training and awareness.

articleTitle: Partial Discharge Diagnostics in Electric Motors Exposed to Ambient Stresses During Industrial Operations
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: In this paper the effect of contamination under varying temperature and relative humidity (RH) in electrical electric motors’ (EM) insulation is investigated through partial discharge (PD) diagnostics. The variations in PD intensity have been investigated under varying environmental conditions. For this purpose, PD measurements were carried out within an artificial industrial environment inside a climate-controlled chamber. Various PD features were extracted to study probability distribution functions to further investigate the PD severity at various levels of contamination, under varying temperatures and RH. Based on the experimental outcomes, it was revealed that PD activity within the EM insulation was significantly affected by temperature and RH under varying contamination conditions. The proposed methodology is believed to be helpful in achieving the desired level of reliability for a wide range of industrial applications exposed to ambient stresses.

articleTitle: Electric Drivers in LNG Liquefaction Plants: Design Aspects and Challenges
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: Over the past five decades within the liquefied natural gas (LNG) industry, there has been a notable evolution in the drivers employed to operate large compressors, encompassing a broad spectrum of solutions such as steam turbines, gas turbines, electric motors, and their combinations. The prevailing trend, influenced by the imperative to mitigate greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, underscores a growing reliance on electric drives.Within an LNG liquefaction plant, the selection of the drivers for refrigeration compressors will significantly determine the overall plant emissions and energy consumption (also known as auto consumption) throughout the plant's life cycle. Utilizing electric motors to power large compressors can notably reduce the carbon footprint of an LNG liquefaction plant, particularly when clean and renewable energy sources (e.g., hydropower, solar, wind) are available.The increasing adoption of electric drivers for high-power LNG compressors necessitates that design engineers carefully consider various design aspects and address unique challenges. A novel concept is introduced for the first time in this paper that explains the torque versus speed capability curves for API 617 [1] specified operating points.A systematic categorization of commercially available high-power electric motors and electric drives based on their type or topology, along with a comparison of their respective performance, serves as a practical guide for selecting an appropriate driver system for LNG applications. Key considerations include grid integration, compatibility between motor and compressor, reliability, availability, and maintenance requirements. This paper delves into these topics in detail.

articleTitle: On-Load Tap Changer (OLTC) Selection and Optimization in Large Power Transformers
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: Large power transformers are critical components of the electrical distribution network in complex energy projects, facilitating the seamless transmission of power across multiple voltage levels. The On-Load Tap Changer (OLTC) is an essential component within these transformers, responsible for regulating the voltage ratios and adapting to variations in load and supply conditions. Three-winding transformers with two secondary windings require regulation taking into consideration the loading on both windings which may be different. Other important parameters that users must consider include selection of impedance to achieve desired short circuit levels downstream, large motor starting, location of tap changer that may impact the size and arrangement of the transformer. This technical paper provides an in-depth review of the function and application of OLTCs, implementation on high voltage (HV) versus low voltage (LV) winding(s), space considerations and optimization strategies for large power transformers. Proper specification and application of the OLTC by users in large power transformers is key to reduce cost, minimize complexity of the design, and bring the best value for the project.

articleTitle: Intelligent Lighting Control for Harsh and Hazardous Areas
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: This paper provides an overview of the value of intelligent lighting control in harsh and hazardous areas. Poor or inadequate lighting is a leading factor in workplace accidents and injuries and this risk increases exponentially in classified environments. Intelligent Lighting Control Systems that offer dimming, scheduling, grouping, daylight harvesting, and occupancy sensing can help optimize lighting throughout a facility and provide the right amount of light at the right time. Apart from helping maintain a safe work environment, these digitally enabled luminaires can help maximize energy savings, meet corporate sustainability goals, and reduce maintenance costs and downtime. By monitoring luminaires remotely and using data and insights from Intelligent Lighting Systems to perform preventative maintenance, facility managers can ensure their luminaires will be serviced in planned maintenance windows before they fail – thus minimizing the time personnel spend in hazardous areas maintaining these luminaires.

articleTitle: Enhancing Success In Carbon Capture Integration With Existing Industrial Facilities: Electrical Challenges And Strategies
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: In a global effort to reduce carbon intensity, heavy industries are actively exploring methods to cut greenhouse gas emissions, with carbon capture emerging as a viable solution. The enactment of the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) of 2022 has made carbon capture economically feasible, thanks to enticing tax incentives aimed at curbing scope 1 emissions. Nonetheless, integrating new carbon capture units into existing industrial complexes presents mechanical, civil, electrical, and environmental challenges. This paper describes the electrical considerations of such projects, addressing hurdles and strategies. Emphasizing early engagement with utilities, it examines their role in managing project costs, schedules, and scopes. Key factors like power requirements, CO2 compressor sizing, and utility transformer procurement are crucial for seamless implementation. Furthermore, it shows the decision-making process concerning the main CO2 compressor, including various starting methods and voltage level selections that significantly impact project costs. Ultimately, this paper aims to provide an electrical perspective to aid in navigating the integration of carbon capture within existing industrial settings.

articleTitle: Lifetime Analysis of Copper and Aluminum Squirrel Cage Rotor of Asynchronous Machines
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: The squirrel cage of the rotor is frequently manufactured using aluminum and its alloys, as well as copper and its alloys. The number of requests from users demanding extended service life has increased, relating to the number of starting cycles. Requests, sometimes far above the conservative specifications existing in API 541 [15], which refers to 5,000 starting cycles. Users are questioning whether a machine equipped with an aluminum squirrel cage rotor, as opposed to a copper cage, can deliver the same performance and longevity when driving the same industrial application. In order to clarify this question, this paper will discuss in depth the performance and lifetime behavior of two squirrel cage motors (6.20 MW and 10.75 MW), one designed with aluminum in the rotor and the other designed with copper. This paper will also compare the environmental impact on the materials, the machine’s overall performance such as efficiency, power factor, torque curve behavior, starting performance and last, but not least, analyzing the number of starting cycles each motor can perform, comparing with API 541 Edition minimum number of starts. Aspects of failure mechanisms will also be addressed.

articleTitle: Modernization of Existing Low and Medium Voltage Switchgear and Motor Control Centers
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: Reliability of the electric supply is largely influenced by the reliability of the major components of the power distribution system. Amongst these, reliability of medium and low voltage switchgear and motor control centers (MCCs) have a key influence on power system reliability. The switchgear and MCCs installed three or four decades ago do not necessarily present the same levels of reliability as modern state-of-the-art equipment. Many end users including utilities and large industrials have older switchgear with air-magnetic or first-generation vacuum switchgear technologies that do not provide the level of arc fault protection which has come to be expected from modern industry standards. As such, this aging equipment does not provide an equivalent level of safety during maintenance and operation when compared to newer equipment. The maintenance issues are also complicated by the lack of spare parts, supply chain interruptions, limited opportunities for maintenance, capital budgets, and lengthy outages associated with the replacement of the aged equipment. Retrofitting, retrofilling or other modifications of the switchgear and MCCs can be more practical, cost effective, and more of an expeditious approach over the replacement of the switchgear. Additionally, modifying the protection, control, and metering, and creating a comprehensive communication network to analyze the data from the new relays, meters and condition monitoring systems allows for further improvements in operation and maintenance as well as successful conversion from time-based to condition-based maintenance programs. This paper addresses the various methods of modernization of low and medium voltage switchgear and MCCs.

articleTitle: Marine Radar Electromagnetic Environmental Effects [E3] on Shipboard and Land Based ASD Operation: Problems and Solutions
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: Field site instances are described where a ship or coastal water radar operation, near an on-ship or land-based crane ASD, caused random software Code Redundancy Check [CRC] faults. Section II characterizes a wide range of radar source emission possibilities in terms of allocated radar frequency ranges IEEE S-band [3 GHz] or IEEE X-band [8 - 12 GHz], peak pulsed power variability [6 to 60 kW pk] and V/m (volts per meter) magnitude at the antenna surface. Section III describes antenna coupling mechanisms from antenna surface to V/m magnitude seen at separated ASD distance. At these frequencies, even small holes in standard ASD grounded metal cabinets allow unattenuated emission internally. Indeed, every opening in the control room door resulted in an immediate CRC trip. Separate research testing, simulating radar high E-fields at unshielded control boards, verified radar operation as the root cause of CRC faults. Existing IEC Radiated Electric Field Susceptibility requirements for land-based ASD only extend to 2.7 GHz and have V/m specifications much lower than those for powerful radar fields in proximity. When standards do not cover unique applications, they are classified as E<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> events. Section IV reviews shielding effectiveness formulas and techniques to use to calculate dBV/m (voltage level in decibels reference to 1v per meter) attenuation levels required at the board level that eliminates radar source issues. Section V ends with a lesson learned summary on how to modify existing standard drive cabinets using an EMC hardened solution checklist on shielding materials and techniques.

articleTitle: Power Management System for a 4 GW Integrated Gasification Combined-Cycle Generation Facility
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: This paper presents the design of a power management system (PMS) for a 4 gigawatt (GW) integrated gasification combined-cycle power plant and refinery. The facility is comprised of 5 combined-cycle power blocks, 800 MW each. The combined-cycle block consists of two gas turbines and one steam turbine. The gas turbine is one of the largest in the world that runs on synthesis gas (syngas). The facility is designed to export 2.4 GW to support the local utility, with the remaining power feeding the refinery and internal loads.The paper discusses the islanding impact on the refinery and how the fast generation-shedding and runback solution maintains power system stability after islanding. Automatic synchronization for the facility to connect back to the local utility at a 380 kV level is also covered in the paper. It also discusses a tie-flow control scheme for active and reactive power at the point of common coupling, dispatched by the local utility or plant operation. This scheme allows utility operators to control demand output at the power block level.The paper covers the automatic black start and load restoration sequence for the facility, a critical requirement and automated within the capabilities of the PMS. Contingency-based load shedding and underfrequency-based load shedding are implemented for the black start substation to ensure the reliability of the black start sequence.The electrical power system, including the syngas turbine challenging modeling, has been tested and validated using hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) simulation.

articleTitle: Coupled Electromechanical Analysis for Torsional Design of Electric Powertrains
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: Calculation procedures are well-established for torsional analyses of industrial powertrains. Usually, the mechanical drivetrain is described by a one-dimensional model, the electromechanical (EME) interaction is neglected, and the electromagnetic loads are included in the solution as external loads. This enables the calculation of electromagnetic loads before the actual torsional analyses. While practical and simplistic, it has been observed that EME interaction may change critical speeds and damping significantly in some applications. The authors main aim is to introduce a coupled EME approach for torsional analyses of industrial powertrains. A fully coupled approach that is systematically compared to the traditional, purely mechanical, analyses and to some intermediate forms of torsional analyses. A calculation example is used to demonstrate the pros and cons of these different approaches based on steady-state, critical speed, harmonic response, short circuit and reclosure analyses. The obtained results will show that the EME interaction is significant when large inertia load is applied, and the first natural elastic frequency is low. A typical industrial application requiring careful torsional analysis is a reciprocating compressor driven by an electric motor with a soft coupling. The largest difference between the un-coupled and coupled analyses was observed in reclosure analyses.

articleTitle: Returns of Experience and Recommendations of Mechanical Integration of Large 2-Pole Variable Speed Electric Motors aor High Availability of Lng Compression Trains
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: Synchronous and asynchronous motor technologies dedicated to high speed make it possible to offer high-power variable-speed compression services without using gearboxes. The mechanical integration of these motors requires special precautions because of the wide speed variation ranges required. The first part of this paper explains the mechanical integration rules described in the API 541 and 546 standards which are the most restrictive in the world, and rotating machines signatures of vibrations in case of mechanical looseness. The main linear and non-linear dynamic mechanisms related to electrical machines are also explained. The second part of this paper describes a site return of experience from a vibratory instability of a 15MW 2-pole starter-helper induction motor and explains the mechanism that led to this instability. The third part of this paper proposes the recommendations to be followed for synchronous or induction motor by manufacturer, OEM, EPC and User-End in terms of modelling, design and testing for successful mechanical integration and high availability, and is illustrated by four business cases: 15MW & 20MW @3 600rpm starter-helper variable speed induction motors fed by Voltage Source Inverter, full electric LNG compression trains driven by 75MW@3000rpm synchronous motors fed by Load Commutated Inverter, including the availability and repairability of the rotating exciter-rectifier device.

articleTitle: The Path to Decarbonization through Electrification: A Refinery Case Study and Lessons Learned
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: The oil and gas industry faces the challenge of strategically becoming more efficient, sustainable, and environmentally responsive. For those industries to achieve that transformation, decarbonizing is one option, and a key solution therein is decarbonation through electrification, a process that involves modifying, upgrading, and/or replacing steam-driven assets with more efficient electrically driven equipment. The electrification process also requires new sources of energy, a robust power system, and possibly even the reconfiguration or upgrade of the electrical distribution. Alternatively, improvement of energy efficiency is another option to rise to these new industry challenges.In this paper, the authors will present a refinery case study using an actual project with close to 40,000 hp of electrification, and improved efficiency, including the path taken from a technical perspective, and the various challenges and lessons learned for a successful execution.

articleTitle: Connectors, Connectors, Connectors: Aren’t they all the Same?
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: Using a connector not rated for the application and improper installation is a cause of power interruption in industrial and commercial facilities. This paper will provide a primer for proper selection and installation practices to improve electrical distribution system reliability and performance. The goal of any electrical system is to perform functionally for the life of the system. This paper will review the types and technical characteristics of electrical connectors that are used for distinct functions within the overall electrical system, such as grounding, bonding, and power connections. Environmental considerations such as direct burial, wet locations, and sunlight resistance will be addressed. Galvanic corrosion will be presented with connector choices and conductor types included. New connector applications such as line side of the service ratings will be introduced. The paper will also address the characteristics of connectors and installation practices for connector applications over 1000 Volts. Connector installation information, such as torque requirements, finely stranded conductor impacts, hole spacing guides per National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA) standard, voltage limitations and temperature rating ampacity impacts will be outlined.

articleTitle: Tool for the Assessment of the Savings in the Cable Acquisition When Employing DC Transmission in Long Distance Drives
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: Throughout different stages of the mining processes, alternating current (AC) motors powered by pulse width modulation (PWM) converters are employed, typically connected by extensive cable lengths. While these drives bring forth significant advantages, they also give rise to challenges associated with high-frequency problems, which, in turn, reduce the operational lifespan of the system components. Off-the-shelf solutions, involving the incorporation of passive filters, tend to adversely affect both the cost and efficiency of the system, justifying research for new alternatives. A recent proposal suggests a distinctive approach, wherein the frequency converter is divided into its rectifier and inverter units. The former is situated in its original location, while the latter is positioned close to the load. Consequently, the drive system operates with direct current (DC) for electric power transmission. This innovative topology not only eliminates the high-frequency problems but also substantially enhances efficiency while reducing costs of the transmission. Prior research has demonstrated the potential of this alternative drive topology, particularly through case studies in low- and medium-voltage systems within mining plants. In this paper, the economic and energy efficiency potentials of such DC transmission drives regarding the power transmission are examined using reference graphs that offer insights beyond conventional case studies. These graphs represent decision-making tools, allowing for a quick and accessible assessment of the economic viability of the alternative topology for a wide range of powers and drive distances. The main aspects related to the methodology, along with relevant technical discussions, are addressed.

articleTitle: Reliability Analysis of IGBT Modules of Multilevel Inverters Operating in Hostile Environments
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: Throughout the industry, pulse width modulation voltage source inverters (PWM-VSI) are commonly utilized with adjustable speed drives (ASD) to control, most commonly, induction motors. Especially in the mining and petroleum industries, long cables connecting motors and inverters are often present, which can cause several problems. As an innovative solution, an alternative system configuration has been previously proposed, in which the rectifier is kept in its typical location, and the inverter bridge and DC bus capacitors are installed near the driven motor. Long cables are used as a DC transmission line, mitigating the high-frequency problems resulting from the inverter-cable-motor interaction. On the other hand, new concerns regarding the reliability of the power devices arise once the inverter is installed in harsh ambient conditions. In this context, this work proposes a reliability analysis of such drive configuration, applying the physics of failure (PoF) approach combined with the design for reliability (DfR) methodology to carry out the design adjustments to achieve the reliability required for the application, focusing on the inverter IGBT modules. Moreover, this paper will evaluate widely accepted multilevel inverter topologies and modulation strategies, verifying those capable of minimizing implementation costs and ensuring adequate reliability indexes for the system—aiming to enable the commercial use of this promising configuration. The results show that a three-level active neutral point clamped inverter (3L-ANPC) topology applying two pulse width modulation (PWM) strategies and 400 A – 6.5 kV IGBTs would be the most appropriate from this study's reliability and feasibility analyses.

articleTitle: Advancement of Safety Features for Industrial Power System Operations and Control
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: For safe operation of electrical systems at various voltage levels, implementation of various interlocks is arguably as important as protective relaying. This paper chronicles the evolution of the various mechanical and electrical interlocks that build inherent safety in the operation of switchgear. This is accompanied by development of complex logics within the protective relays and their communications over fiber-optic networks that reduce the number of required control cable installations, the potential points of physical failure, and the ongoing maintenance effort. The paper begins with an overview of the industry practice common to most balanced, polyphase power systems. This is followed by specific features that apply to various types of switchgear.A case study of a state-of-the-art interlock system on a large oil and gas facility, where every electromechanical action of the switchgear interlocks is mimicked by the power management system, is discussed. This includes not only the mechanisms present within the switchgear at each voltage level, but those necessary across various voltage levels.This paper aims to simplify the understanding of power system interlocks and their interactions with protection and control systems by providing rule-of-thumb guidelines and innovative solutions incorporated in modern power systems, improving operational safety and reliability of the power systems.

Author Keywords: Hierarchy of Controls for Hazard Mitigation

articleTitle: A Comparison of Protection based ARC Flash Mitigation Techniques
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: Reducing the exposure and risk to arc flash in medium voltage switchgear is an important mission for industrial facilities. Several arc flash mitigation techniques are available using modern microprocessor-based protective relays. This paper will review and compare various protective relay based applications such as zone selective interlocking (ZSI) scheme, high impedance bus differential protection scheme, low impedance bus differential protection scheme, light and current sensing scheme, and maintenance / alternate setting scheme.

articleTitle: High Voltage Circuits in Large Industrial Facilities
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: This paper provides insight into the impact on the facility electrical circuit distribution voltages resulting from the significant increase in power demand of large industrial facilities. Historically the high voltage circuits for industrial facilities were limited to the point of connection with the local utility; however, with the shift in power demand, it is now commonplace for these facilities to utilize high voltage power distribution within the plant boundary. This shift in power demand is primarily related to the need to accommodate an entirely electric driven production model. EPC firms are traditionally accustomed to distribution systems using cable with voltages up to 35kV in which the underground and above ground cable design allows additional flexibility for cable routing. This paper will highlight how underground and above ground designs using large high voltage cable require additional considerations for the planned cable routing, offsets, transition points, pull points, and installation methods. Furthermore, the paper will highlight the advantages of having a joint team of the engineer, the installer, and the cable manufacturer working together early in the project design stage is critical and how this early collaboration and planning can minimize changes in the design as the project moves into the execution phase. The paper will provide recommendations on the discussion points that need to be investigated at the onset of high voltage underground design for an in-plant power distribution system. Lastly, this paper will present a case study of a 138kV underground distribution within a large LNG facility and highlight the key considerations implemented during the design phase which resulted in improved constructability and ease of cable pulling/installation.

articleTitle: Alarm Management Fundamentals – What is the Impact of Electrical Equipment Automation on Industrial Control Systems
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: Poor alarm management is one of the leading causes of unplanned downtime, contributing to over $20B in lost production every year [1], and of major industrial incidents such as the one in Texas City (2005). Developing good alarm management practices is not a discrete activity, but more of a continuous process (i.e., it is more of a journey than a destination). This paper will describe the ISA 18.2 standard "Management of Alarm Systems for the Process Industries" [2]. Example alarm considerations for intelligent motors/motor controls, drives, and electrical infrastructure integrated into process control systems will also be discussed as well as why electrical engineers who implement IEC 61850 [3] substation automation systems need to adhere to alarm management standards.ISA 18.2 provides a framework and methodology for the successful design, implementation, operation, and management of alarm systems and will allow end-users to address one of the fundamental conclusions of Bransby and Jenkinson that "Poor performance costs money in lost production and plant damage and weakens a very important line of defense against hazards to people." [4].

articleTitle: Trans-Alaska Pipeline System—Improved Safety and Reliability Via Main-Tie-Main, Arc-Flash, and Fast Bus Protection Schemes Using IEC 61850 Over a Software-Defined Network
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: An 800-mile long pipeline system transports North Slope crude oil from Prudhoe Bay across the State of Alaska to Valdez. The Valdez Marine Terminal is the northernmost ice-free port in North America, where tankers are loaded to deliver the critical crude oil supply to market. The operator of this pipeline system requires a reliable, safe, and redundant power supply for efficient and safe operation. Any electric power disruption and the associated downtime severely impacts the flow of oil through the pipeline and the loading of the tankers. The electric power reliability and safety is improved via a custom main-tie-main scheme, along with an arc-flash and fast bus protection scheme, using the high-speed IEC 61850 Generic Object-Oriented Substation Event protocol. This solution is also implemented with cybersecurity best practices that are resilient to external threats using a software-defined network supporting a zero-trust architecture and security gateways. This paper dives deeper into the objectives, design philosophy, communications architecture, and testing procedure for this solution. The scheme is standardized and successfully commissioned into service at Valdez Marine Terminal for one medium-voltage and two low-voltage switchgear facilities in 2019. This innovative solution is then scaled to include further switchgear facilities from 2019 to the present.

articleTitle: Power System Design Considerations for an Island Combined Cycle Power Plant for an Electrical LNG Facility
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: A safe and reliable power system is integral to the success of a project. Electrical power system configuration is designed and developed during the early design phase of a project. Critical decisions must be made early on with limited information considering factors such as - cost, reliability, and risk. This paper discusses electrical design considerations for an island power system supplying an electric Liquified Natural Gas (eLNG) facility.The paper will focus on early design phase aspects offering general guidelines based on authors’ experience, on electrical power system design, generator modeling, Sub-synchronous Tortional Interaction (SSTI), transient stability and power management system aspects that need to be considered for design of a large complex power system with Brownfield tie-ins.

articleTitle: Optimization Techniques of Substation Capability Applying Natural Ester Liquid-Filled Transformers
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: Natural ester liquids, applied as insulating liquids, have demonstrated performance improvements in power transformers. While the early adopters were motivated by the fire safety and improved environmental footprint, the main driver nowadays is the increased thermal class of the insulating paper when immersed in natural ester fluids. This allows increasing the temperature rise limits without compromising transformer life and reliability. This paper expands this benefit beyond the transformer capability ("a variable performance box") providing analysis of the system wide impact (outside the box). Thanks to the fact that the same system demand can be supplied through a natural ester transformer having a base rating lower than what would be required if using mineral oil, with the adjacent components, system configuration and overall protections optimized accordingly. The main discussed impacts will be IEEE transformer standards compliance; transformer average winding temperature rise versus life and reliability; medium voltage switchgear costing; weight reduction for floating ship production operation; civil engineering construction cost reduction; N-1 designs; questionable need for fire walls and suppression systems between transformers; medium voltage power cable cost reductions; total installed system cost reduction.

articleTitle: Settings Management with IED-Integrated Reporting Leads to Enhanced System Benefits
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: Device settings management, associated with the 500 MW expansion of an existing oil and gas facility’s 250 MW power system incorporating approximately 12,000 protective relays and other intelligent electronic devices, requires careful planning, defined commissioning processes, and meticulous change management administration. However, once systems are in place, loss-of-production events due to settings errors or relay manufacturer defects can be minimized in duration or eradicated completely when compared to traditional settings management methods.This paper presents an overview of the expanded power system, including intelligent electronic device-communications data flow, settings database structure, settings management, including the inventory of firmware and serial numbers, and an automated, facility-wide intelligent electronic device event report collection, as well as several examples in which automated, integrated reports resulted in a faster system restoration than was previously available at the facility. Sample events that resulted in an accelerated system restoration include a greenfield construction-area loss of source, a 60 MVA transformer energization, and the incorrect current transformer polarity leading to a line differential relay trip event.

articleTitle: Load-Side Voltages on Open Low-Voltage Circuit Breakers Due to Parasitic Capacitive Coupling
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: The unavoidable parasitic capacitance that exists between circuit breaker contacts can cause an ac voltage to exist on the load side of an open circuit breaker. While this phenomenon is well-known for high-voltage circuit breakers, it also exists for low-voltage circuit breakers but is not as well documented. With the proliferation of trip units capable of measuring voltage, if the load-side voltage is monitored the operator may be surprised to see such a voltage on the load side of an open circuit breaker and this may raise safety concerns. This paper explores this phenomenon in detail, describing the system conditions that affect the voltage level encountered, the means to lower such voltages, and the safety impact.

articleTitle: Lithium-Ion Battery Systems: Risk Management, Operations and Maintenance Considerations
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: For typical industrial UPS and switchgear control applications, oil and gas, refinery, petrochemical, and offshore platform operations are beginning to transition from vented lead acid (VLA), valve regulated lead acid (VRLA), and nickel cadmium (Ni-Cd) batteries to modern battery technologies. Recognize that modern battery technologies require battery management and control systems that were not mandatory for VLA, VRLA, or Ni-Cd technologies.Lithium-Ion (Li-ion) papers and presentations tend to highlight and promote the "advantages," while providing only an overview of the Battery Management System (BMS). To increase awareness and understanding, the author’s’ previous paper "Lithium-Ion BMS Concepts for Industrial UPS Applications and Questions We Should Be Asking" [1] focused on the BMS systems for a conceptual example Li-ion battery system used with a typical 120V industrial UPS with backup power in range of 15kVA to 200kVA and stored energy greater than 20kWh. This paper conveyed to PCIC an overview and understanding of the BMS systems.This paper will focus on Lithium-Ion (Li-ion) battery operational and risk management considerations, factory acceptance testing (FAT), shipping, storage, commissioning, operation, and maintenance.

articleTitle: Replacing Electromechanical Relays With Microprocessor Relays to Provide Thermal Protection for Motors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: Thermal overload protection is a critical part of any motor protection scheme. Older electromechanical relays provide thermal protection with an inverse-time overcurrent element. Replacing electromechanical relays with modern microprocessor-based relays requires the development of settings for a more sophisticated thermal protection element, such as the first-order thermal model. Additionally, this requires a planned outage to install the new relay and commission the settings. To correctly set the thermal element in a microprocessor-based relay, motor manufacturer data (such as a nameplate, data sheet, and system data) are needed. However, these data are not always available for older motors. This paper describes the settings required for the first-order thermal model and provides case studies from various end users illustrating how settings from existing electromechanical relays were used to develop settings for a microprocessor-based thermal element.

articleTitle: Reliable and Efficient High Power DC Distribution for Hydrogen Electrolysis
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: Hydrogen is a versatile fuel source, and electrolysis stands out as a promising method to produce hydrogen. Traditionally, the power distribution system for hydrogen electrolysis is designed for the individual electrolyzer modules with DC (direct current) power requirement in the range of 1 to 5 MW. The power supply to these modules is accomplished in three steps starting from high voltage to medium voltage and medium voltage to low voltage transformations. The last step involves the rectification process from AC power to DC power to electrolyzers. Supplying DC power to a gigawatt-scale hydrogen plant comprises of multiple power transformers, rectifier transformers and rectifiers in parallel leading to larger footprint, and higher capital and higher maintenance costs. Accordingly, this paper explores an alternative approach, where high-power DC distribution system, like those used in aluminum potlines, for hydrogen production. These are proven technologies used for long time in mining and metals industry. Operational experience of such a system highlights its reliability, efficiency, cost-effectiveness, and enhanced adaptability. This paper addresses the critical role of high-power DC distribution systems in realizing the full potential of hydrogen electrolysis for sustainable energy production..

articleTitle: Can High-Efficiency LV Motors Be Rewound While Maintaining Their Original Premium Efficiency Levels?
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: High-efficiency LV motors are becoming more prevalent, even replacing old plant motors. The main drivers for this are legislative requirements to reduce electricity consumption, increased electricity costs, and pressure to reduce carbon footprints. But even when each motor has a lower power rating, there are often thousands of these LV motors installed in a typical petrochemical plant. This begs the question: Can high-efficiency LV motors be rewound while maintaining their original premium efficiency levels?This paper explains the high-efficiency motor design and components and evaluates the influence on performance of different repair levels; e.g., basic repairs, stator rewinds, core damage and rotor damage. Case studies are presented showing when repairs can maintain efficiency, when they can’t, and instances where the repair can increase efficiency. The paper concludes that it is definitely possible to repair a high-efficiency LV motor while maintaining or even improving efficiency.

articleTitle: Harmonic Suppression for Matrix Converter Based AC Drives
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: Using matrix converters for AC-to-AC power conversion provides economy on weight and size, high reliability and efficiency. For these reasons, the matrix converter technology is currently being adopted in underground mining applications (such as variable speed AC drives for underground vehicles). This paper treats harmonic issues around the matrix converter operation, such as transfer of the supply side distortions to the load and the injection of excessive current harmonics into the supply. The paper explores fundamental limitations to the harmonic performance and proposes a flexible control scheme that provides harmonic compensation at both the supply and the load sides of the matrix converter. Several strategies are formulated and tested. An optimized combination of the harmonic suppression at both sides is achieved. This makes matrix converter-based drives suitable for power systems with weak supply and voltage distortions. The presented ideas are validated by simulations.

articleTitle: Overvoltages in Medium Voltage Industrial Systems Associated with Switching High Voltage Transformers Connected Through Insulated Cables
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: This work presents and discusses the solutions to overvoltages experienced by the medium voltage system (13.8 kV) in an existing refinery resulting from the switching of power transformers supplied by a high voltage system (230 kV) through insulated cables. The analysis demonstrates the influence of the other feeder cables and the transient interaction between them and the switched feeder, due to their high capacitances, leading to the increase of overvoltages to values over the insulation withstand. These overvoltages exhibit high frequency and high amplitude and are primarily transferred from the high voltage side to the medium voltage side mainly through transformer capacitive couplings. This process may lead to insulation breakdown in medium voltage equipment, as confirmed by simulations and practical observations. Solutions for overvoltage mitigation, such as surge arresters and pre-insertion resistors applied to switching circuit breakers, are presented.

articleTitle: IEEE 1017 Family of ESP Cable Standards – A Major Update
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: The 2021 Published Versions of IEEE Recommended Practice (RP) 1017.1, RP1017.2 and RP1017.3 (formerly RP1017, RP1018 and RP1019) contain the most significant modifications to the documents since their initial publication in 1984. Version 5 (the 2021 version) includes greatly expanded content and a complete revamp of the group of Recommended Practices. All three RPs were expanded to include 8 kV rated cable in addition to the 3 kV and 5 kV historic rated voltages. Additionally, cable sizes were expanded to include #3/0 AWG and #4/0 AWG. RP 1017.1 was expanded to include all testing: factory, acceptance, and field testing. Additionally, advanced test methods including very low frequency tan-delta (VLF tan-delta) and partial discharge (PD) were included, along with interpretation guidance. Testing for surface feedthroughs and downhole connectors was added. New tests for qualification of encapsulating materials for non-lead metallic barrier cables with encapsulating jacket were also added. RP 1017.2 and RP 1017.3 were modified to include non-lead metallic barrier cables (sometimes called "tubing encapsulated power cable" or "TEPC"). The insulating and jacket material specifications were expanded to include reinforced high modulus materials. Finally, the Neher-McGrath curves were updated to correct an error and to make them more readable and usable.

articleTitle: Use of Predictive Analytics on a Critical Heated Pipeline
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Technical Conference (PCIC)
abstract: This paper presents a case study of the application of predictive analytics using a fiber-optic based temperature monitoring system on an electrically heat traced asphalt pipeline at a refinery in North America. A skin-effect trace heating system and a fiber optic Distributed Temperature Sensing (DTS) system was installed on an approximately 700m long section ("DTS zone") of an asphalt pipeline passing over various railroads and highways. The piping upstream and downstream of the DTS zone was only heat traced but not monitored by a DTS system (i.e., outside of the DTS zone).
